result:
I used to think freedom was a space. A wide-open field, a desert highway at midnight, a room with the door left unlocked. It took me a long time to understand that freedom is actually a practice, and like any practice it is mostly repetition, mostly showing up when you don't feel like it, mostly choosing to keep your hands in the work even when the work feels pointless.

I learned this in a kitchen at 3:17 a.m. in a town that no longer exists on any map I trust. I was twenty-three and I had just moved into an apartment above a laundromat on a street where the streetlights had a habit of going out one by one until the whole block was lit only by the flicker of dryers through the floorboards. The apartment had a kitchen the size of a confession booth. One window that looked out onto a fire escape and the brick wall of the building next door. A two-burner stove, a refrigerator that hummed in B-flat, and a table that wobbled on three legs.

That night I couldn't sleep. The laundromat below was closed but the machines were still warm, and the heat rose through the floor and made the apartment feel like a sauna. I made tea. I made too much tea. I sat at the wobbling table with a notebook and a pen that was running out of ink and I told myself I would write for ten minutes and then go to bed.

Ten minutes became an hour. The hour became three hours. I was not writing anything good. I was writing the grocery list I had meant to write, the email I was afraid to send, the argument I had with my mother in 2011 about why I wasn't married yet, the way the light looked on the brick wall at 3 a.m. when it was only illuminated by the red EXIT sign across the alley. I wrote about the sound the refrigerator made and how it reminded me of my grandfather's breathing when he was asleep in his recliner. I wrote about the fact that I was afraid of becoming the kind of person who only writes about fear.

That is the thing about free writing. If you tell yourself you can write about anything, you will inevitably write about the thing you most want to avoid. The mind is a polite host. It offers you the neutral, the interesting, the clever. And then it slides the real plate to you under the tablecloth.

I kept writing because the alternative was to lie there in the heat and listen to the dryers breathe. There is a particular kind of honesty that only emerges when you have removed all the reasons to be good. No audience. No deadline. No style guide. No word count. The instruction had been simple: write freely about whatever you want. And so I did. I wrote about the scar on my left knee from when I fell off a swing set at seven. I wrote about how I still check the weather for a place I haven't lived in for eight years. I wrote about the way my father folds his t-shirts into perfect squares and how that small act of order feels like love.

Somewhere around page four I started to notice something shifting. The sentences stopped trying to impress. They got shorter, then longer again, then they started to loop back on themselves like a trail in the woods. I began to hear my own voice in the writing, not the voice I use in meetings or in texts or in the careful way I speak to people I like. This voice was tired. It was a little mean. It was also kind in a way I didn't expect.

It said: you are not behind. It said: the fact that you are awake at 3 a.m. writing about a refrigerator does not make you a failure. It makes you a person who is paying attention.

I think we confuse attention with productivity. We think if we are not making something that can be sold or liked or shared, we are wasting time. But attention is the first form of care. To sit with a subject long enough to notice its grain, its color, the way it catches light at a particular angle, is to love it in the smallest, truest way. I had been paying attention to that kitchen for weeks and I had not really seen it until I was forced to write it down.

The kettle whistled. I had forgotten it was on. The tea had gone cold. The pen had finally given up. I closed the notebook and the apartment was still hot and the dryers were still breathing below me. I did not feel transformed. I did not feel enlightened. I felt, for the first time in a long time, un-alarmed. The night was still the night. The work was still the work. But I had spent a few hours in a place where the only requirement was to be accurate.

That is a strange kind of freedom.

Later in life I moved to cities with better streetlights. I got a job with deadlines and Slack channels and performance reviews. I learned how to write for an audience, which is a skill, a real skill, and also a kind of costume. You learn which words make people nod, which anecdotes make them feel something, which sentences they will screenshot and send to a friend. You learn to edit yourself before you even start.

But once a year, usually in late August when the heat sits low in the air and the nights are too warm to sleep, I find myself back at that wobbling table. Sometimes it's literally a table. Sometimes it's a laptop at a kitchen counter in a different apartment with a different refrigerator hum. I open a blank document and I give myself permission to write badly. I write about whatever comes. I write about the way the light falls on the brick. I write about the scar on my knee. I write about the t-shirts folded into squares.

And every time I do it, I remember that the point was never to produce something. The point was to practice being in the room with myself without flinching.

Freedom, I think now, is not the absence of constraints. It is the ability to choose your constraints consciously. The 2500-word essay, the ten-minute timer, the notebook with a dying pen, the kitchen at 3 a.m. — these are all constraints. They make the freedom possible. Without a boundary, the mind wanders in circles until it exhausts itself. With a boundary, the mind can go deep.

There is a Japanese concept called shibumi, which is hard to translate. It is the art of effortless perfection, the kind of beauty that doesn't call attention to itself. A stone in a garden. A well-made chair. A sentence that does exactly what it needs to do and then stops. I think of free writing as the opposite of shibumi. It is deliberately un-shibumi. It is messy, repetitive, embarrassing. It is the practice that makes shibumi possible because it clears the throat.

I have spent years collecting notebooks. They are full of starts. The first page of each one is always good. By page three the handwriting gets sloppier. By page ten there is a coffee ring and a doodle of a cat and a phone number I will never call. People ask me if I ever reread them. I do, sometimes, when I'm sick or when the heat gets into the apartment again. I don't read them for the good lines. I read them for the evidence. The evidence that I was here. That I kept paying attention.

If you give a person a blank page and no instructions, most people will freeze. The blank page is terrifying because it is infinite. So we need a prompt. Write about your childhood. Write about a color. Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words. The prompt is a door. It doesn't tell you where to go, it just tells you the door is unlocked.

I have tried to carry that lesson into other parts of life. When I am anxious, I ask myself: what would it look like to write about this for ten minutes without trying to solve it? When I am angry, I try to describe the anger the way I would describe a weather pattern. When I am in love, I try to notice the small, stupid details — the way they tap their foot when they are thinking, the way they say the word "actually" too often.

It doesn't always work. Sometimes I just end up with a list of complaints. But the practice is not about getting it right. The practice is about staying in the room.

There is a moment in every long piece of writing where you hit the wall. Around word 800, maybe 1200. The initial excitement is gone. The ideas are thin. The sentences start to sound like sentences you have read before. This is the moment most people quit. They close the laptop and tell themselves they will come back tomorrow. And sometimes that's fine. But sometimes you have to push through the wall because the wall is where the real stuff is.

On the other side of the wall, the writing gets stranger. You start making connections that don't make sense to anyone else. You start writing about the refrigerator and suddenly you are writing about your grandfather and suddenly you are writing about death and suddenly you are writing about how the red EXIT sign looks like a small, tired heart. It feels embarrassing. It feels true.

I think that is what people are afraid of when they are asked to write freely. They are afraid of what will come out when no one is editing. They are afraid they will discover they are boring, or cruel, or sadder than they thought. They are afraid they will discover they are more alive than they thought.

Both are possible. Usually both are true.

If you have never tried it, try it. Tonight, if you can, make a cup of tea and sit down with a piece of paper. Set a timer for twenty minutes. Don't worry about grammar. Don't worry about making sense. Write about the room you are in. Write about the sound the refrigerator makes. Write about the last time you felt embarrassed. Write about the color of the streetlight outside your window. If you get stuck, write "I don't know what to write" until you know what to write.

You will find that the words come. Not always good words. But words. And after twenty minutes you will have something that is yours in a way that very little else is. It won't be perfect. It will be honest.

And honesty, at 3 a.m. in a kitchen above a laundromat, feels a lot like freedom.

I am still not sure what to do with all those notebooks. Maybe one day I will type them up. Maybe one day I will burn them. Probably I will just keep them in a box under my bed, where they can be found by someone I love after I am gone, and they will think I was a better writer than I was. Or they will think I was a sadder person than I was. Or they will just see the evidence: I was here. I paid attention. I kept writing.

The night is getting lighter now. The red EXIT sign is fading as the sky turns grey. The dryers below have finally stopped. The refrigerator is still humming in B-flat. I have been writing for a long time. The page is full. The pen is dead. The tea is cold.

I think this is enough.

I think this is what it means to be free: to sit down, to begin, to keep going even when it's messy, to stop when the light comes up, and to know that you can always come back tomorrow and start again.
